authority_standard: CURRENT official primary/government authority only (malegislature.gov for MGL; official Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy 247 CMR publications hosted by mass.gov). No secondary, commercial, or study-site sources were used or relied upon.

questions.reasoning: 247 CMR 9.01(2) forbids processing a prescription or dispensing a drug, device or other substance 'in a manner which is intended, either directly or indirectly, to circumvent any law or regulation governing the practice of pharmacy.' The prohibition attaches to the MANNER and expressly reaches INDIRECT circumvention, so step-by-step facial compliance of each transfer is no defence. The regulation contains no element of patient harm and no element of financial gain, which disposes of the harm-based and gain-based options. Because the sequence was designed to put the patient in possession of a supply the pharmacy could not lawfully have dispensed directly, the arrangement is a violation.

247 CMR 9.01(14) states flatly that 'A licensee may not provide any practitioner with blank prescription forms which refer to any pharmacist or pharmacy.' The prohibition is unconditional: it has no element of an agreement, no element of remuneration or anything of value, and no element of actual patient steering. The separate anti-kickback standard in 247 CMR 9.01(11) is not the operative provision here. Supplying pads printed with the pharmacy's own name and address to a prescriber therefore violates 9.01(14) notwithstanding the absence of any agreement, consideration or referral, and the prohibition is not confined to controlled substances.

247 CMR 16.04(6) requires that 'An authorized pharmacist must maintain a COPY of the current CDTM agreement, including copies of current patient referral and patient consent, in the primary practice setting, readily retrievable at the request of the Board of Registration in Pharmacy and Board of Registration in Medicine.' That single sentence supplies four requirements: a copy of the current agreement (B), inclusion of copies of the current patient referral and patient consent (C), maintenance in the primary practice setting (D), and ready retrievability on request (E). Option A is wrong and is in fact the inverse of the rule: the same provision directs that the SUPERVISING PHYSICIAN maintains the original of the agreement, referral and consent in the patient's medical record in the physician's custody, so the pharmacist holds copies, not the signed original.

The pharmacist is wrong on both points. 247 CMR 16.04(6) requires the documents to be readily retrievable at the request of the Board of Registration in Pharmacy AND the Board of Registration in Medicine, so a Board of Registration in Medicine investigator may demand them; 247 CMR 16.05 reinforces that nothing in 247 CMR 16.00 limits the Board of Registration in Medicine's review, monitoring and investigation of its licensees' activities. The same provision requires the supervising physician to maintain the ORIGINAL of the current CDTM agreement, including the original current patient referral and patient consent, in the patient's medical record in the physician's custody. The physician therefore could not properly hand the original to the pharmacist for safekeeping; the original belongs in the physician's record.

247 CMR 16.04(3) provides that 'A collaborative practice agreement shall specify those duties of the authorized pharmacist that may be delegated to other appropriately trained and authorized staff and those duties under the agreement that shall not be delegated.' Delegation authority is therefore affirmative and agreement-sourced: it must be written into the agreement in both its positive form (D) and its negative form (E). Silence cannot operate as permission (A). Neither the delegate's training (B) nor the characterisation of vital-sign collection as a non-dispensing act (C) supplies the authority that only the agreement can confer; the technician's training is a necessary condition for a permitted delegation, not an independent source of it.

247 CMR 16.04(3) imposes two distinct drafting duties. The first sentence requires the agreement to name delegable and non-delegable duties, which this agreement has done. The second sentence adds that 'A collaborative practice agreement shall specify WHEN AND HOW an authorized pharmacist may delegate duties under the agreement, and the DURATION AND SCOPE of the delegation.' That second requirement is unmet, so the agreement is not yet complete (A is wrong). The regulation nowhere requires Board pre-approval of a particular delegation (B), a separate patient consent to delegation (D), or the supervising physician's countersignature on the delegation instrument itself (E).

MGL c.112 s.24B-1/2(e) provides that 'No retail pharmacy may employ a physician for the purpose of maintaining, establishing or entering into a collaborative practice agreement with a patient' but that 'Nothing shall prohibit a retail pharmacy from hiring a physician or licensed medical practitioner for the purpose of conducting quality assurance reviews of its pharmacists that are engaged in the practice of collaborative drug therapy.' 247 CMR 16.04(7)(b) and (c) reproduce the same split. The two engagements are therefore treated oppositely: the quality assurance review engagement is expressly permitted and the collaborative-practice-agreement engagement is expressly prohibited. The prohibition is categorical, so tying the physician's pay to something other than prescription volume (D) cannot cure it.

MGL c.112 s.24B-1/2(a) defines 'Patient' as 'a person who is referred to a pharmacist by his supervising physician' and adds that 'The supervising physician shall assess the patient and include a diagnosis when referring the patient to the collaborating pharmacist' (C) and that 'The patient shall be notified of, and shall consent to, the collaborative drug therapy management services in the retail drug business setting' (E); a community pharmacy is the retail drug business setting, and 247 CMR 16.03(5)(c) requires a written referral specifying the primary diagnosis plus the patient's written informed consent. A patient's own report of what her physician said (A), her self-presentation (B), and the pharmacist's unilateral file note of the conversation (D) none of them supply the physician-originated assessment, diagnosis and referral the statute requires.

MGL c.112 s.24B-1/2(a) closes the definition of 'Patient' with the direction that 'Individual referral and consent shall be recorded by the pharmacist and the supervising physician in the patient's record.' The obligation is conjunctive as to actor and single as to location: both professionals must record, and the place of recording is the patient's record. 247 CMR 16.03(5)(d) says the same, requiring the authorized pharmacist and supervising physician to maintain a written record of both the individual referral and the written informed consent in the patient's records maintained by each of them. The physician's assurance that his own chart entry suffices is therefore wrong (A), as are the pharmacist-only (B), professional-election (C) and Board-register (E) options.

The written-referral requirement is setting-specific, not universal. 247 CMR 16.03(5)(c)1. imposes a written referral only in the community pharmacy (retail drug business) setting, and 247 CMR 16.04(1)(a) likewise conditions the community pharmacy CDTM agreement on 'a written referral of a specific patient.' By contrast 247 CMR 16.03(1) and MGL c.112 s.24B-1/2(c)(1) subject hospital CDTM only to approval by the hospital medical staff executive committee or designee and impose no individual written referral. A documented discussion with the attending supervising physician about that specific patient therefore constitutes a referral in the hospital setting, whereas the community pharmacist lacks the written referral her setting requires. Options D and E overstate the rule by making writing, or signature, universal.

MGL c.112 s.24B-1/2(a) defines collaborative drug therapy management as 'the initiating, monitoring, modifying and discontinuing of a patient's drug therapy by a pharmacist in accordance with a collaborative practice agreement' (A), and provides that it 'may include: collecting and reviewing patient histories' (B); 'obtaining and checking vital signs, including pulse, temperature, blood pressure and respiration' (C); and 'under the supervision of, or in direct consultation with, a physician, ordering and evaluating the results of laboratory tests directly related to drug therapy' (E). The same clause closes with the express limit that the evaluation 'shall not include a diagnostic component,' which excludes D; settling a diagnosis is outside CDTM however plainly a laboratory result appears to support one.

MGL c.112 s.24B-1/2(a) permits a collaborating pharmacist to order and evaluate laboratory tests directly related to the drug therapy, but only 'under the supervision of, or in direct consultation with, a physician' and 'when performed in accordance with approved protocols applicable to the practice setting and when the evaluation shall not include a diagnostic component.' On these facts the ordering satisfies every condition attached to it, so the ordering may be proper and option B is wrong. The evaluation, however, concluded that the patient has a new condition, which is precisely the diagnostic component the statute excludes, so C is wrong. The bar on diagnosis is absolute and is not cured by onward reporting to the supervising physician, which disposes of E; and D is wrong because laboratory work is expressly within CDTM.

247 CMR 16.04(5) imposes two sequenced duties on termination or non-renewal. The first is anterior: 'PRIOR TO termination or non-renewal of a CDTM agreement, an authorized pharmacist and supervising physician shall arrange for an uninterrupted continuation of the patient's drug therapy.' The second is the written notice to the patient of the termination and of the continuation procedures. Because the agreement lapses at the end of the month and nothing has yet been arranged, it is the anterior duty to arrange uninterrupted continuation before the lapse that has already been missed. Option A is wrong because post-lapse notice cannot discharge a duty that had to be performed beforehand. The regulation requires no advance notice to the Board (B) or to other prescribers (C), and a written extension (D) is not a duty at all.

247 CMR 16.03(5)(c)1. requires a written referral but prescribes no writing medium, and Massachusetts treats indelible pencil as a permanent writing medium: MGL c.94C s.23 provides that written prescriptions 'shall be written in ink, indelible pencil or by other means.' A referral in indelible pencil therefore satisfies the writing requirement (D) and option A, which would confine writing to ink, is wrong. Separately, 247 CMR 16.04(6) requires the current patient referral to be maintained 'readily retrievable' at the request of the Board of Registration in Pharmacy and Board of Registration in Medicine. A flattened image the pharmacy system can neither store nor retrieve in readable form fails that requirement (E), so B is wrong: electronic transmission may be permissible in principle but does not rescue a referral that cannot be retrieved in readable form. C is wrong because no handwritten signature is prescribed for a CDTM referral.

MGL c.94C s.21A permits the counselling obligation to be satisfied by a toll-free telephone service where the person elects delivery of a prescription drug at a location other than a pharmacy, but attaches a specific mechanical condition: 'The number of such toll-free telephone service shall be printed on a label AFFIXED TO EACH CONTAINER of a prescription drug dispensed by a pharmacy to a patient.' Here the number appears only on enclosed delivery paperwork and nowhere on the containers, so the statutory condition fails. Options A and B ignore that express placement requirement. D is wrong because home delivery does not require a face-to-face offer, and E is wrong because a toll-free service is expressly an approved method.

MGL c.94C s.21A directs that the pharmacist record 'any additional comments relevant to the patient's drug use, including any failure to accept the pharmacist's offer to counsel,' and then supplies the evidentiary consequence of silence: 'The absence of any record of a failure to accept the pharmacist's offer to counsel shall create a presumption that such counseling WAS PROVIDED.' The presumption runs in the pharmacy's favour, so silent records are not merely neutral (A) and do not raise an adverse presumption (C). Because the statute resolves the question by presumption, the pharmacy need not fall back on the dispensing pharmacist's recollection (D). E is wrong because the statute requires recording of a refusal, not affirmative recording of counselling given.

MGL c.112 s.24B-1/2(a) defines a collaborative practice agreement as 'a written and signed agreement between a pharmacist with training and experience relevant to the scope of the collaborative practice and a supervising physician' (A), and adds three further constitutive features: 'The collaborative practice shall be within the scope of the supervising physician's practice' (B); 'Each collaborative practice agreement shall be subject to review and renewal on a biennial basis' (C); and 'A collaborative practice agreement shall include individually developed guidelines for any prescriptive practice of the pharmacist' (E). D is wrong: neither the statutory definition nor 247 CMR 16.00 makes filing with the Board a precondition to acting, and 247 CMR 16.04(6) instead requires a copy to be maintained in the primary practice setting readily retrievable on Board request.

247 CMR 9.17(3) provides that 'The DUR shall be based upon CURRENT standards which MAY include the following,' then lists four named works and closes with '(e) other peer-reviewed medical literature.' Two things follow. The list is permissive and non-exhaustive, and its final item expressly embraces peer-reviewed literature beyond the named works, so a current peer-reviewed journal article is a proper basis (B) and options A and C, which would confine reliance to the named works, are wrong. Separately the governing adjective is 'current': being a named compendium does not preserve a superseded edition, so the superseded edition fails (E) and D is wrong.

247 CMR 9.17(2) provides that upon identifying a problem on prospective review 'a pharmacist shall take appropriate measures to ensure the proper care of the patient which may include consultation with the prescribing practitioner,' and then adds a freestanding record duty: 'A pharmacist shall document any measures taken in response to a drug utilization review.' Clinically resolving the therapeutic duplication discharges the first duty but not the second, so A is wrong. The regulation requires no report of a therapeutic duplication to the Board (B), no repeat prospective review of the revised therapy (C), and no written confirmation from the prescriber of an agreed change (D). What remains outstanding is the documentation of the measures taken.

247 CMR 9.01(15) provides that 'A licensee may not refuse to compound simple or moderate NON-STERILE compounded preparations customary to the community needs except upon extenuating circumstances or by a waiver of Board regulation.' The first refusal falls squarely inside that duty: the preparation is a simple non-sterile oral suspension customary to the community, the pharmacy holds the equipment and ingredients, and a stated preference not to compound is neither an extenuating circumstance nor a Board waiver, so the refusal is prohibited. The second request is for a STERILE preparation, which the provision does not reach at all, so that refusal falls outside the duty rather than being affirmatively permitted by a general freedom to choose services (A) or prohibited (B). The duty is fixed by the community's customary needs, not by what a neighbouring pharmacy could have done (E).

247 CMR 9.01(9) provides without qualification that 'A licensee may not engage in any fraudulent or deceptive act.' Deception is framed as the wrong itself, so the rule contains no element of reliance (D), no element of loss, and no element of financial gain (E). Literal accuracy of each individual entry does not save an arrangement designed to induce a conclusion the pharmacist knows to be untrue, because it is the arranging that is deceptive, so A is wrong. B is wrong because 9.01(9) operates independently of the dispensing rules; compliance with those rules is not a defence to a separate deceptive act.

247 CMR 9.01(16) imposes two obligations: 'A licensee shall maintain patient confidentiality and PROTECT a patient's confidential information.' The second limb is affirmative and protective, so the duty is not confined to refraining from disclosure, and A fails. Leaving completed prescriptions face up on an open counter and displaying a printed waiting list of patient names to everyone in the queue is a failure to protect, and the breach is complete on exposure; whether anyone is shown to have read the information goes to consequences, not to breach, so B fails. C is wrong because a consultation area, required by 247 CMR 9.18(6) for counselling privacy, does not license leaving identifiable information on open display. D is wrong because the duty is owed continuously and does not await a complaint.

247 CMR 9.01(7) provides that 'A pharmacy SHALL accept a medication that it previously dispensed to a patient if the medication: (a) was dispensed to the patient in error; or (b) is suspected to be defective or contaminated,' and closes with the converse: 'A pharmacy is not required to accept a medication from a patient that was properly dispensed and not defective at the time it was dispensed.' The first return, of the wrong strength, was dispensed in error and must be accepted; the second, correctly dispensed and not defective, need not be. The quarantine and disposal rule in the same provision governs what happens to a medication after it is accepted and is not a ground for declining it, so D inverts the rule. B and C ignore the express division, and E is wrong because an accepted medication may not be returned to inventory at all.

247 CMR 9.06(3) provides that 'A pharmacy that dispenses a naloxone rescue kit or other approved opioid antagonist shall provide counseling AND the opioid antagonist information pamphlet AT THE TIME OF DISPENSING,' which supplies both A and B as to the first requestor. 247 CMR 9.06(4) provides that 'A pharmacy that does not have a naloxone rescue kit or other approved opioid antagonist readily available for dispensing at the time requested SHALL REFER the requestor to the nearest location that has [one] readily available,' which supplies C and confirms E: unavailability is the trigger for the referral duty, not an excuse from it. D is wrong because inviting the second requestor to return another day substitutes a deferral for the mandatory referral.

MGL c.94C s.19B(e) fixes both the person and the timing. It requires the pharmacist to 'treat the transaction as the dispensing of a prescription to the person PURCHASING the opioid antagonist REGARDLESS OF THE ULTIMATE USER,' which makes the mother, not the absent son, the relevant insured; and it provides that 'Unless the person purchasing the opioid antagonist requests to pay for the prescription out-of-pocket, the pharmacist or designee shall make a reasonable effort to identify the purchaser's insurance coverage and to submit a claim for the opioid antagonist to the insurance carrier PRIOR TO DISPENSING.' Since she did not ask to pay out of pocket, her coverage must be pursued and the claim submitted before supply. E is wrong because the statute expressly contemplates purchase for another person.

MGL c.94C s.21A provides that 'The pharmacist or his designee shall make REASONABLE EFFORTS to obtain, record and maintain' patient information including 'individual history where significant, including known allergies and drug reactions.' The standard is one of effort, not of achieved completeness, so an identical gap in two profiles can produce different outcomes. Asking on three separate visits and being refused is a reasonable effort, so the first pharmacy is compliant (D); never asking because the queue was long is no effort at all, so the second is not (E). A is wrong because it applies the effort standard to a pharmacy that made none, B is wrong because completeness is not the test, and C is wrong because the stem holds the missing history identical in both cases, so clinical significance cannot be the discriminator.

247 CMR 9.01(4) states that 'A pharmacist shall practice pharmacy within the scope of his or her education, training, and experience AND within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice.' The requirement is conjunctive: general professional authorisation is necessary but not sufficient, and the pharmacist's own education, training and experience form an independent limit. Because she has never been trained in the technique and has never performed it, the individual limb fails even though the profession-wide limb is satisfied, which defeats A. An employer's direction cannot enlarge a licensee's personal competence (B). Observation by a trained colleague (C) is not a substitute the regulation recognises, and D is wrong because the Board issues no individual authorisation of this kind; the cure is training, not dispensation.

247 CMR 9.01(17) provides that a pharmacist 'may not practice in a pharmacy for more than 12 hours IN A 24 HOUR PERIOD without completing an eight consecutive hour rest period prior to resuming work,' which supplies the measurement window in E. It continues: 'In the event of an extenuating circumstance, a pharmacist ... may exceed 12 hours IN ORDER TO ACT IN THE BEST INTEREST OF THE PATIENT, provided the time in excess of 12 hours is MINIMIZED and the licensee DOCUMENTS the extenuating circumstance.' That single proviso yields A (the extenuating-circumstance, patient-interest route is the only authorised basis), B (minimisation) and C (documentation). D is wrong because a district manager's instruction is a commercial direction, not a regulatory authority, and cannot itself supply the exception.

247 CMR 9.01(17) conditions the lawful excess: having practised more than 12 hours in a 24 hour period, a pharmacist may not resume work in a pharmacy 'without completing an EIGHT CONSECUTIVE HOUR rest period prior to resuming work in a pharmacy.' The operative word is consecutive. Four hours of rest, then a shift in an unrelated setting, then five further hours does not produce an unbroken eight-hour block, so aggregating to nine hours does not satisfy the rule and A fails. The regulation prescribes no twenty-four hour break (C) and no notification to the Board (D). E fails because documenting the extenuating circumstance legitimated the fourteen-hour shift itself but does not displace the separate rest requirement that follows it.

MGL c.94C s.21A provides that 'A pharmacist shall conduct a prospective drug review before each new prescription is dispensed OR DELIVERED to a patient or a person acting on behalf of such patient,' which establishes C and simultaneously refutes B, since delivery to the patient or to the patient's agent is expressly covered and no personal attendance is required. The statute continues that 'Such review MAY INCLUDE, BUT NOT BE LIMITED TO, screening for potential drug therapy problems due to therapeutic duplication ...', which establishes D and refutes A: the enumerated items are permissive and expressly non-exhaustive rather than the whole of the duty. E is refuted by the text of the same sentence, which includes 'drug interactions, INCLUDING SERIOUS INTERACTIONS WITH NONPRESCRIPTION OR OVER-THE-COUNTER DRUGS.'

The two standing-order regimes differ precisely in the mood of their training clauses. MGL c.94C s.19A(d) provides that 'Before dispensing emergency contraception authorized under this section, a pharmacist MAY complete a training program approved by the commissioner,' so training is permissive and its absence is no bar. MGL c.94C s.19E(c) provides that 'before dispensing a COVID-19 drug authorized under this section, a pharmacist SHALL complete a training program approved by the commissioner,' a mandatory condition precedent. An untrained pharmacist may therefore dispense emergency contraception under the statewide standing order but may not dispense the COVID-19 drug. D wrongly makes training mandatory for both, C wrongly makes it optional for both, and E substitutes a notification the statutes do not provide.

247 CMR 9.01(12) provides that 'A licensee may not dispense or distribute any EXPIRED, outdated, defective, contaminated, counterfeit, contraband, or otherwise substandard drug or device to any person or entity WHO IS NOT LICENSED OR LEGALLY AUTHORIZED to receive such drug or device.' The prohibition turns on the recipient's licensure or legal authorisation, not on the product's condition or on disclosure. A licensed reverse distributor is authorised to receive expired stock, so that transfer may proceed. A volunteer overseas aid group that is not licensed to receive drugs is not, and a pharmacy technician wanting stock for training purposes is not a person legally authorised to receive it, so both are prohibited. Telling recipients the product has expired (B) is irrelevant to the test, and E overstates the rule by barring the authorised route as well.

247 CMR 9.01(3) provides that 'UNLESS OTHERWISE REGULATED BY THE BOARD, a licensee shall adhere to the MOST CURRENT standards established by each chapter of the United States Pharmacopeia.' The provision does two things. It makes currency the operative requirement, so following a years-old edition on a point the Board has never regulated fails even though a genuine USP chapter was followed: D is correct and A is wrong. It also subordinates USP to Board regulation by its opening clause, so where a Board regulation addresses the point differently the Board regulation displaces USP: E is correct and B is wrong. C is wrong because the provision incorporates USP generally rather than requiring chapter-by-chapter Board adoption.

legal_uncertainty_flags.note: The writing-medium point is not addressed by 247 CMR 16.00, which requires only a 'written referral'. The proposition that indelible pencil is an acceptable permanent writing medium in Massachusetts pharmacy practice is taken from MGL c.94C s.23, which governs written prescriptions rather than CDTM referrals. The selection is nevertheless secure because options A, B and C are each affirmatively refuted (no ink-only rule exists for referrals; the emailed referral fails 247 CMR 16.04(6) ready retrievability; no handwritten signature is prescribed), leaving D and E. Flagged for confirmation against the canonical rule record at Phase 3A.

In accordance with the authority standard, the official 247 CMR PDFs were obtained through browser access to the official Massachusetts government source and their text extracted in-page. 247 CMR 9.00 as retrieved carries the official revision stamp 12/6/24; 247 CMR 16.00 carries the official date 12/15/2017. No secondary, commercial, aggregator or study-site source was used or relied upon for any determination.
